topics.title: Chapter 59 — System Robustness
topics.summary: Robustness is the ability to behave predictably when inputs are invalid, resources are unavailable, operations make partial progress, or dependencies fail. It requires explicit failure contracts and cleanup paths. A robust system does not have to succeed at every request; it must avoid turning a failed request into corruption, leakage, or an unexplained hang. Correctness on the normal path is only the beginning. Examine each resource acquisition and each externally visible update: what can fail before it, what can fail after it, and what state remains when that happens?

topics.title: 59.1 Defensive programming
topics.summary: Defensive programming validates assumptions at trust boundaries and makes internal invariants explicit. Validate external lengths, indexes, versions, and resource requests before using them. Keep validated values in a representation that will not silently change during later conversion. Avoid indiscriminate checks that conceal programming errors or continue with fabricated defaults. A failed invariant inside a component may require stopping that operation rather than proceeding with a “best guess” pointer or size. The response should preserve safety and make diagnosis possible.

topics.title: 59.2 Error handling
topics.summary: Error handling must define the operation’s postcondition after failure. Did nothing happen, did some bytes transfer, or did the update commit but its acknowledgment fail? These are different states with different retry rules. Design for idempotence where retries are expected. Repeating a read is different from repeating a money transfer or appending a record. An error does not necessarily mean that the remote side performed no work. Protocols need identifiers, transactions, or explicit reconciliation when duplicate effects would be harmful.

topics.title: 59.3 Return values
topics.summary: Use each interface’s documented failure indicator. A negative descriptor result, a null allocation result, MAP_FAILED , a short element count, and a C++ exception are not interchangeable conventions. Some APIs return an error number directly rather than storing it in errno , notably many POSIX thread interfaces. Reading errno after such a call can report an unrelated value. Wrap interfaces only after preserving their distinct contracts.

topics.title: 59.4 errno
topics.summary: errno is meaningful when an interface documents that its failure result sets it. A successful call need not clear an old error value. Inspecting errno after success can therefore diagnose a failure that never occurred. Save the error code before cleanup or logging that could change it. Report the failed operation and relevant safe context, not just an unexplained number. In multithreaded POSIX environments, errno access is thread-specific, but that does not make stale values meaningful. [ R54 ]

topics.title: 59.5 Assertions
topics.summary: Assertions document and test internal invariants. They are not a substitute for validating untrusted input because ordinary C/C++ assertion checks can be disabled in builds defining NDEBUG . Do not place required side effects inside an assertion. assert(close(fd) == 0) can remove the close operation when assertions are disabled. Perform the operation explicitly, handle its result, and use assertions only for checks whose removal does not change required behavior.

topics.title: 59.6 Sanitizers
topics.summary: AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and ThreadSanitizer instrument different classes of behavior. Their availability, compatible combinations, and runtime requirements differ. Address and undefined-behavior checks are commonly combined; thread-race checking should normally use a separate build. [ R5 , R6 , R53 ] A clean run means that the enabled instrumentation reported no covered failure during that execution. It does not prove memory safety, race freedom, or correct recovery on unexecuted paths. Keep compiler warnings, static analysis, boundary tests, and design review alongside instrumentation.

topics.title: 59.7 Resource cleanup
topics.summary: Cleanup releases every owned resource exactly once: memory, descriptors, mappings, threads, temporary files, and permits. RAII in C++ and structured cleanup paths in C make the ownership visible during both normal returns and failures. Destructors should not casually throw during stack unwinding. Operations whose completion can fail meaningfully, such as flushing durable output, often need an explicit checked completion method before fallback destruction. Cleanup that merely prevents leaks is not the same as successful commit.

topics.title: 59.8 Failure recovery
topics.summary: Recovery establishes a known consistent state after failure. Common techniques include constructing a new result before replacing the old one, writing temporary files before rename, logging transactions, and restarting isolated workers. Atomic visibility and durable persistence are different guarantees. A rename can make a new pathname visible atomically under filesystem rules, while durable recovery after power loss can require synchronizing the file and containing directory. The exact guarantee also depends on filesystem and hardware behavior. [ R33 ]

topics.title: Worked example — A checked snapshot protocol in a private temporary directory
topics.summary: The program below creates its own temporary directory, writes a new snapshot, synchronizes it, closes it, renames it into place, and synchronizes the directory. It then verifies the bytes and removes only its own test artifacts. It does not operate on an existing user file. Companion listing: ch59/snapshot.c The expected output is snapshot checks passed on a filesystem supporting the requested synchronization. The test verifies successful API sequencing and byte contents. It does not simulate power loss, prove a storage device’s behavior, or establish crash consistency on every filesystem. The commit point also matters for real recovery. If rename succeeds but directory synchronization fails, the new file may already be visible even though the requested durability was not confirmed. A production API should report that distinction instead of promising that failure means “nothing changed.” This private test removes its own artifacts after either path, which is appropriate for a lab but not a replacement for an application’s recovery policy.

SLIDE 1: Chapter 59 — System Robustness

LECTURE NARRATION
Robustness is the ability to behave predictably when inputs are invalid, resources are unavailable, operations make partial progress, or dependencies fail. It requires explicit failure contracts and cleanup paths. A robust system does not have to succeed at every request; it must avoid turning a failed request into corruption, leakage, or an unexplained hang. Correctness on the normal path is only the beginning. Examine each resource acquisition and each externally visible update: what can fail before it, what can fail after it, and what state remains when that happens?

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.
